title: VO₂max and performance: the three-factor model
goal: Use Joyner and Coyle's model (VO₂max × fractional utilisation × economy) to predict race speed or power, and explain why VO₂max predicts performance poorly among elite athletes.

steps.title: Three numbers make a speed
steps.text:
Joyner and Coyle put endurance performance into one model built from three factors [[c:jc-model]]:

**[performance VO₂](g:performance-vo2) = VO₂max × [fractional utilisation](g:fractional-utilisation)**

**speed or power = performance VO₂ × economy**

- **VO₂max**: the ceiling.
- **Fractional utilisation**: the share of that ceiling you can hold for the race. Your [lactate threshold](g:lactate-threshold) sets most of it.
- **Economy**: how much speed ([running economy](g:running-economy)) or power ([gross efficiency](g:gross-efficiency)) each litre of O₂ buys.

Performance VO₂ is the oxygen you can keep using for the race; economy turns it into speed. Raise any of the three and you go faster.

claims.text: VO₂max and the lactate threshold together set the performance VO₂ that can be sustained; efficiency (economy) sets the speed or power produced at that VO₂.

evidence.quote: Efficiency interacts with the performance .VO(2) to establish the speed or power that can be generated at this oxygen consumption.
Running economy and fractional utilization of VO2max also affect endurance performance.

steps.title: How much of the ceiling you can use
steps.text:
The longer the race, the smaller the share of VO₂max you can hold: about 75–85% in a marathon, 90–100% over 10 km, close to 100% over 5 km [[c:jc-fractions]].

The share depends mostly on where blood lactate starts to climb. Untrained people see the upturn at about 60% of VO₂max; trained people can usually work at 75–85% before a marked rise [[c:jc-lt]].

This can separate riders whose VO₂max is the same. Fifteen cyclists, all near 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, rode an hour as hard as they could in the lab. Their 1 h power tracked the VO₂ at their lactate threshold (r = 0.93), and the elite group rode 40 km on the road 10% faster than the state-level group [[c:coyle1991]].

steps.title: From VO₂max to race speed
steps.problem: A runner has a VO₂max of 60 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. She can hold 85% of it for a 10 km race, and her running costs 200 mL·kg⁻¹ per km. How fast can she run?
steps: Speed = performance VO₂ ÷ cost per km = 51 ÷ 200 = 0.255 km per minute. The mL·kg⁻¹ cancel, leaving km·min⁻¹.
× 60 for km·h⁻¹: 0.255 × 60 = 15.3 km·h⁻¹, about 39 min 13 s for 10 km.

steps.title: Economy: how far each litre goes
steps.text:
At the same running speed, the oxygen cost can differ by about 30–40% between people [[c:jc-economy-range]].

That difference shows most when VO₂max is similar. Conley and Krahenbuhl tested 12 men who all placed in the top 19 of a national 10 km race. Their VO₂max averaged 71.7 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ and did not predict their times (r = −0.12). Running economy did: it explained 65% of the spread in 10 km time [[c:conley]].

Cycling shows the same trade-off. In 11 world-class road cyclists, those with the lowest VO₂max had the highest efficiency (r about −0.7): a high efficiency seemed to make up for a lower ceiling [[c:lucia]].

claims.text: The oxygen cost of running at a given speed varies by about 30–40% between individuals.

evidence.quote: The oxygen cost of endurance running (ml kg min −1 ) at a given speed can vary about 30–40% among individuals

claims.text: Among 12 highly trained runners of similar ability, VO₂max was unrelated to 10 km time (r = −0.12) while running economy explained 65% of the variation.

evidence.quote: The relationship between Vo2max and distance running performance was r = -0.12 (p = 0.35).
Within this elite cluster of finishers, 65.4% of the variation observed in race performance time on the 10 km run could be explained by variation in running economy.

claims.text: In world-class cyclists, VO₂max correlated inversely with cycling economy and gross efficiency: a high efficiency seems to compensate for a relatively low VO₂max.

evidence.quote: A high CE/GE seems to compensate for a relatively low VO2max in professional cyclists.

steps.title: Why VO₂max predicts poorly among elites
steps.text:
So does VO₂max hardly matter? No. A runner with a VO₂max of 80 will beat one with 40 over 5,000 m. Across a wide range of people VO₂max is tied closely to endurance performance; the link only blurs when everyone tested has a similar, high value [[c:levine-range]].

That blur is [range restriction](g:range-restriction). Pick only people with a high VO₂max, and VO₂max hardly differs between them, so what still varies, threshold and economy, decides the result. VO₂max sets the upper limit: you can't race above 100% of it for long. It is the entry ticket; the other two settle the race.

The speed at the lactate threshold combines all three factors, which is why it is the best single lab predictor of distance-running performance [[c:bh-vlt]].

claims.text: VO₂max is closely tied to endurance performance across a wide range of people; the relationship is obscured when only elite athletes with similar values are compared.

claims.text: VO₂max sets the upper limit for endurance performance; the speed at the lactate threshold integrates VO₂max, economy and fractional utilisation and is the best physiological predictor of distance-running performance.

evidence.quote: VO2max is an important variable that sets the upper limit for endurance performance (an athlete cannot operate above 100% VO2max, for extended periods).
The speed at lactate threshold (LT) integrates all three of these variables and is the best physiological predictor of distance running performance.

steps.title: The same model on the bike
steps.text:
On a bike, economy is [gross efficiency](g:gross-efficiency): the share of the energy from each litre of O₂ that reaches the pedals. One litre of O₂ releases about 20.5 kJ (*Energy expenditure* module). So:

**power (W) = performance VO₂ (L·min⁻¹) × 20,500 ÷ 60 × GE**

The ÷ 60 turns J per minute into J per second, which is watts.

The model explains why two riders with the same VO₂max can be far apart in a time trial. A rider who holds 90% instead of 80%, or rides at 23% efficiency instead of 21%, gains about 10–13% in power (90 ÷ 80 = 1.125; 23 ÷ 21 = 1.095): worth a minute or two over 40 km [[c:jc-model-bike]].

claims.text: VO₂max and the lactate threshold set the sustainable performance VO₂; efficiency sets the cycling power produced at that VO₂.

evidence.quote: and lactate threshold interact to determine the ‘performance .VO(2)’ which is the oxygen consumption that can be sustained for a given period of time.

steps.title: From VO₂max to time-trial power
steps.problem: A cyclist has a VO₂max of 4.5 L·min⁻¹, holds 85% of it for a 40 km time trial and rides at a gross efficiency of 22%. What power can he hold?
steps: Metabolic power = 3.825 × 20,500 J per L ÷ 60 s = about 1,307 W.
Power at the pedals = 1,307 × 0.22 = about 288 W.

points: Joyner and Coyle: performance VO₂ = VO₂max × fractional utilisation; speed or power = performance VO₂ × economy.
Fractional utilisation falls with race length (marathon about 75–85% of VO₂max) and is set mostly by the lactate threshold.
Economy differs by 30–40% between runners; among athletes of similar VO₂max, economy and threshold decide the result.
VO₂max predicts poorly among elites because of range restriction, not because it doesn't matter; it sets the upper limit.
Speed at the lactate threshold combines all three factors and is the best single lab predictor of distance-running performance.

variants.stem: Over a winter, a runner's VO₂max stays the same, but the pace he can hold for an hour rises because his lactate threshold moves from 80% to 86% of VO₂max. Which factor of Joyner and Coyle's model changed?

options.why: Right: he can now hold a bigger share of the same ceiling, raising his performance VO₂.
The stem says VO₂max stayed the same.
Economy is the O₂ cost of a given speed; nothing here says it changed.

options.text: None: pace can't rise without a higher VO₂max
options.why: Pace can rise through either of the other two factors, as here.

variants.stem: A cyclist's VO₂max and threshold are unchanged after a bike fit, but she now holds 8 W more at the same oxygen uptake. Which factor of the model changed?

options.why: Right: more watts from the same litres of O₂ is better efficiency.
Her threshold, and so the share of VO₂max she can hold, didn't change.
The stem says VO₂max is unchanged.
Performance VO₂ (VO₂max × fraction) is the same; it now buys more watts.

variants.stem: A runner with a VO₂max of 60 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ races a marathon. What average oxygen uptake can she most likely sustain?

options.why: Right: a marathon is run at about 75–85% of VO₂max: 0.75–0.85 × 60.
That is 95–100% of VO₂max, a 5 km intensity; it can't be held for over 2 hours.
50–60% is an easy run; trained runners race marathons well above that.
No one can work at 100% of VO₂max for long; the marathon is raced below it.

variants.stem: A triathlete with a VO₂max of 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ runs a stand-alone 10 km race all-out. What average oxygen uptake can he most likely sustain?

options.why: Right: 10 km is raced at about 90–100% of VO₂max.
75–85% is marathon intensity, too low for an all-out 10 km.
50–60% would be an easy training run.

options.text: More than 70, since racing raises VO₂max
options.why: Racing can't take VO₂ above its maximum.

variants.stem: Two groups of cyclists have the same VO₂max (about 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹), yet one rides a 40 km time trial 10% faster. Their 1 h power tracks the VO₂ at their lactate threshold. What best explains the gap?

options.text: The faster group can hold a bigger share of the same VO₂max
options.why: Right: with equal ceilings, a higher threshold raises the performance VO₂, and with it power.

options.text: The faster group must really have a higher VO₂max
options.why: The stem says VO₂max was the same; the gap comes from what they can sustain.

options.text: The slower group was less motivated on the day
options.why: Their 1 h power tracked a physiological measure, the VO₂ at the threshold, not just effort.
Lean body mass didn't differ, and on flat time trials absolute watts matter most.

variants.stem: A runner's VO₂max is 55 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. She can hold 80% of it for a half marathon, and her running costs 200 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹. What speed can she hold?

options.why: This uses the whole VO₂max (55 ÷ 200 × 60), forgetting the 80%.
This is km per minute; multiply by 60 for km·h⁻¹.
This applies the 80% twice (55 × 0.8 × 0.8).

variants.solution: Performance VO₂ = 55 × 0.80 = 44 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Speed = 44 ÷ 200 = 0.22 km·min⁻¹ = 13.2 km·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: A runner's VO₂max is 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. He can hold 90% of it for 10 km, and his running costs 210 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹. What speed can he hold?

options.why: This uses the whole VO₂max (70 ÷ 210 × 60), forgetting the 90%.
This is km per minute; multiply by 60 for km·h⁻¹.
This applies the 90% twice (70 × 0.9 × 0.9).

variants.solution: Performance VO₂ = 70 × 0.90 = 63 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Speed = 63 ÷ 210 = 0.30 km·min⁻¹ = 18.0 km·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: A triathlete's VO₂max is 65 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. She can hold 85% of it for a stand-alone 10 km run, and her running costs 190 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹. What speed can she hold?

options.why: This uses the whole VO₂max (65 ÷ 190 × 60), forgetting the 85%.
This is km per minute; multiply by 60 for km·h⁻¹.
This applies the 85% twice (65 × 0.85 × 0.85).

variants.solution: Performance VO₂ = 65 × 0.85 = 55.25 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. Speed = 55.25 ÷ 190 = 0.291 km·min⁻¹ = 17.4 km·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: Two runners can both sustain 54 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ for a race. Runner A's running costs 190 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹, runner B's 210. Who is faster, and by about how much?

options.text: B, as using more O₂ means a bigger engine
options.why: B uses more O₂ per km, so the same O₂ supply carries him less far.

options.text: Neither, since their performance VO₂ is equal
options.why: Equal O₂ supply gives equal speed only if economy is equal too.
The costs differ by 20 out of about 200, which is about 10%, not 20%.

variants.stem: Two cyclists can both sustain 4.0 L·min⁻¹ of VO₂ for a time trial. Rider A's gross efficiency is 23%, rider B's 21%. Who holds more power, and by about how much?

options.why: Right: power is proportional to efficiency at the same VO₂: 23 ÷ 21 = 1.095, about 314 vs 287 W.

options.text: B, as a lower efficiency means more O₂ used
options.why: Both use the same O₂; A turns more of it into power.

options.text: Neither, since their performance VO₂ is equal
options.why: The same O₂ gives more watts at a higher efficiency.
Two percentage points out of 21% is a 9.5% relative difference, not 2%.

variants.stem: In 11 world-class road cyclists, those with the lowest VO₂max had the highest efficiency. What is the best reading?

options.text: Among pros, high efficiency can make up for a lower VO₂max
options.why: Right: to reach world class you need enough of the product; riders get there with different mixes.

options.text: A high VO₂max makes a cyclist less efficient
options.why: A correlation in 11 selected riders can't show that one causes the other.

options.text: Efficiency matters more than VO₂max for everyone
options.why: This is a narrow, selected group; across all riders VO₂max varies hugely and matters a lot.

options.text: VO₂max doesn't matter in professional cycling
options.why: All of them had high values (about 72); the trade-off shows only within that high range.

variants.stem: A blog cites a study of 12 elite 10 km runners in which VO₂max didn't predict race time (r = −0.12), and concludes: "VO₂max doesn't matter for running." What is the best critique?

options.text: Range restriction: all had similar, high VO₂max values, so it couldn't show its effect
options.why: Right: across a wide range of runners VO₂max is closely tied to performance; within a narrow elite band it can't separate them.

options.text: Correlation can't show cause, so no conclusion is possible
options.why: True in general, but the key flaw is the narrow range, which hides a real relationship.

options.text: 10 km is too short a race for VO₂max to matter
options.why: A 10 km is run at 90–100% of VO₂max; VO₂max matters there.

options.text: An r of −0.12 means VO₂max slows runners down
options.why: It is close to zero and not significant; it shows no link in this group, not a harmful one.

variants.stem: A paper on 10 professional cyclists finds that VO₂max doesn't predict time-trial results. A coach concludes that VO₂max tests are pointless for his club riders. What is the best judgement?

options.text: Flawed: pros all have similar VO₂max; club riders vary widely
options.why: Right: range restriction in a pro sample doesn't carry over to a varied club.

options.text: Sound: what is true for pros is true for everyone
options.why: Results in a narrow, selected group don't generalise to a much wider range.

options.text: Sound: only economy matters in cycling
options.why: Economy matters, but VO₂max sets the ceiling all the factors work within.

options.text: Flawed: the study should have used runners
options.why: The sport isn't the problem; the narrow range of VO₂max is.

variants.stem: According to Bassett and Howley, which single lab measure best predicts distance-running performance?

options.text: The running speed at the lactate threshold
options.why: Right: it combines VO₂max, fractional utilisation and economy in one number.
VO₂max sets the ceiling but leaves out how much of it you can use and at what cost.
HRmax says nothing about the ceiling's use or the cost of running.

options.text: Blood lactate at the end of a ramp test
options.why: Peak lactate reflects anaerobic effort at the end, not sustainable speed.

variants.stem: A cyclist has a VO₂max of 5.0 L·min⁻¹, can hold 85% of it for an hour, and rides at 22% gross efficiency. Using 20,500 J per litre of O₂, what power can he hold?

options.why: This uses the whole VO₂max (5.0 L·min⁻¹), forgetting the 85%.
This is the metabolic power; only 22% of it reaches the pedals.
This forgets to divide by 60: J per minute aren't watts.

variants.solution: Performance VO₂ = 5.0 × 0.85 = 4.25 L·min⁻¹. 4.25 × 20,500 ÷ 60 = 1,452 W metabolic. × 0.22 = about 320 W.

variants.stem: A triathlete has a VO₂max of 4.0 L·min⁻¹, can hold 80% of it for the bike leg, and rides at 21% gross efficiency. Using 20,500 J per litre of O₂, what power can she hold?

options.why: This uses the whole VO₂max (4.0 L·min⁻¹), forgetting the 80%.
This is the metabolic power; only 21% of it reaches the pedals.
This forgets to divide by 60: J per minute aren't watts.

variants.solution: Performance VO₂ = 4.0 × 0.80 = 3.2 L·min⁻¹. 3.2 × 20,500 ÷ 60 = 1,093 W metabolic. × 0.21 = about 230 W.
